queue.claim: Skeletal ageing sizes used as priors: the maxillary, glabellar and pyriform angles fall by single-digit degrees between young and old cohorts, and the orbital aperture grows in area and width, with the most recession superomedially and inferolaterally (Shaw and Kahn 2007; Kahn and Shaw 2008). These set maxilla_retrusion 0–10 deg (sigma 3) and orbit_rim_recession 0–3 mm.
queue.query: Shaw Kahn aging midface bony elements CT maxillary angle glabellar angle pyriform angle degrees young old

queue.claim: The mandible ages by losing ramus height, body height and body length while the gonial angle opens a few degrees (Shaw et al. 2010). Most of the change follows tooth loss, and after extraction the mandibular ridge loses height several times faster than the maxillary ridge (Tallgren 1972).
queue.query: Shaw 2010 aging of the mandible aesthetic implications gonial angle ramus height dentate edentulous

queue.claim: Resting upper-incisor display falls from about 3 mm in the 20s to about 0–1 mm by the 60s, roughly 0.5–1 mm per decade (Vig and Brundo 1978). This gives the prior mu = max(0, 3 - 0.07*(age-25)) mm.

queue.claim: Ears lengthen about 0.2 mm a year in adults (Heathcote, BMJ 1995). A library source instead says ear size and shape hold steady until about age 70.
